clinicalPearls: Rare autosomal recessive deficiency of coagulation factor V, historically termed parahaemophilia or Owren disease.
Deficiency prolongs both the prothrombin time and the activated partial thromboplastin time because factor V acts in the common pathway.
Bleeding is predominantly mucocutaneous, with epistaxis, gum bleeding, menorrhagia and bleeding after surgery or trauma; severe cases may have deeper bleeds.
Around a fifth of total factor V is stored in platelet alpha-granules, and platelet factor V levels may modify the bleeding phenotype.
Because plasma-derived factor V concentrate is not widely available, fresh frozen plasma is the mainstay of replacement; platelet transfusion can supply factor V in refractory bleeding.
An acquired form occurs, often from autoantibodies triggered by bovine thrombin exposure, surgery, infection or malignancy.
Combined factor V and factor VIII deficiency is a distinct disorder caused by defects in the LMAN1 or MCFD2 intracellular transport proteins.
Distinguish inherited factor V deficiency from factor V Leiden, an unrelated prothrombotic mutation causing activated protein C resistance.
reference.pathophysiology: Factor V is a large plasma cofactor that circulates in an inactive form and, once activated by thrombin or factor Xa, serves as the essential non-enzymatic cofactor of the prothrombinase complex. In that complex activated factor V dramatically accelerates the factor Xa-mediated conversion of prothrombin to thrombin on phospholipid surfaces, so its deficiency markedly reduces thrombin generation and prolongs both the prothrombin time and the activated partial thromboplastin time. Inherited deficiency, due to mutations in the F5 gene, is usually autosomal recessive and may reduce factor V synthesis or produce a dysfunctional protein; roughly one fifth of the body's factor V is held within platelet alpha-granules and released locally at sites of injury, which helps explain why bleeding severity correlates imperfectly with the plasma level. A clinically important separate entity is combined deficiency of factors V and VIII, caused not by defects in either factor gene but by loss of function of the LMAN1-MCFD2 cargo receptor that chaperones both proteins through the secretory pathway. Acquired factor V deficiency reflects inhibitory autoantibodies, classically after exposure to topical bovine thrombin but also with surgery, infection, autoimmune disease or malignancy, and its clinical impact ranges from an incidental laboratory abnormality to life-threatening haemorrhage.
additionalDifferentials: Factor X deficiency and other common-pathway factor deficiencies
Combined factor V and factor VIII deficiency (LMAN1/MCFD2 defect)
Vitamin K deficiency, vitamin K antagonist effect or liver disease
von Willebrand disease and platelet function disorders for mucosal bleeding
additionalInvestigations: Prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time (both prolonged)
Mixing study to detect an acquired factor V inhibitor
Concurrent factor VIII assay to identify combined factor V and VIII deficiency
Assays of other clotting factors to exclude liver disease or vitamin K-related deficiency
Bethesda-type inhibitor titre where an acquired inhibitor is suspected
F5 (and LMAN1/MCFD2) genetic testing with family studies
redFlags: Intracranial or other central nervous system haemorrhage, particularly in neonates
Major surgical, gastrointestinal or postpartum bleeding
Sudden severe bleeding suggesting an acquired factor V inhibitor
Bleeding poorly responsive to fresh frozen plasma
reference.prognosis: Most inherited cases have a mild to moderate bleeding tendency and a good outlook when replacement is provided around surgery, trauma and childbirth. Acquired factor V inhibitors have a more variable course, from spontaneous resolution to severe haemorrhage, with prognosis influenced by the underlying trigger.
pitfalls: Confusing factor V deficiency (a bleeding disorder) with factor V Leiden (a thrombotic mutation)
Missing combined factor V and factor VIII deficiency by not measuring both factors
Failing to consider an acquired inhibitor after bovine thrombin exposure or surgery
Relying on plasma factor V levels alone when platelet-stored factor V modifies bleeding
Expecting a dedicated factor V concentrate to be available when plasma or platelets are usually required
references: United Kingdom Haemophilia Centre Doctors' Organisation guidance on rare bleeding disorders (standard reference)
